title: Understanding netstat
description: Displays active TCP/UDP connections, listening ports, routing table, interface statistics, and per-protocol statistics to help diagnose network and port usage on Windows.
summary: Displays active TCP/UDP connections, listening ports, routing table, interface statistics, and per-protocol statistics to help diagnose network and port usage on Windows.

examples.description: Lists all connections and listening ports with numeric addresses and the owning process ID (PID). Useful to identify which PID has a port open.
Filters numeric output to show connections/listeners on TCP/UDP port 80. Helpful for confirming HTTP port usage or conflicts.
Shows all connections/listeners with the executable (-b), numeric addresses (-n), and PID (-o). Requires elevation; useful for mapping ports directly to binaries.
Displays the IP routing table (same as route print). Use this to verify default gateways and route precedence.
Shows TCP protocol statistics only. Useful for spotting retransmissions, resets, and overall TCP health.
Displays all connections and listening ports and attempts to resolve foreign addresses to FQDNs. Helpful when you need human-readable remote endpoints.

important_fields.description: Shows all connections and listening ports. Essential when verifying whether a service is actually listening.
Disables DNS/FQDN lookups and shows numeric addresses. Avoids delays and makes scripting/filtering predictable.
Displays the owning process ID. Critical for correlating ports to processes for remediation.
Displays the executable creating each connection or listener. Often requires elevation; invaluable for identifying the exact binary.
Filters by protocol (TCP, UDP, TCPv6, UDPv6, IP, IPv6, ICMP, ICMPv6). Reduces noise and focuses analysis.
Output column indicating protocol (TCP or UDP). Helps separate connection-oriented vs connectionless traffic.
IP and port bound locally (0.0.0.0 or [::] means all interfaces). Key for exposure/scope of a listening service.
Remote endpoint IP/port. Identifies who you are connected to or receiving from.
TCP connection state (LISTENING, ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT, CLOSE_WAIT, etc.). Indicates lifecycle/health of connections.
Owning process identifier (with -o). Needed to map ports to processes via tasklist or Task Manager.
Shows the routing table. Useful for validating default route and specific network paths.
Displays per-protocol statistics. Helps quantify errors, resets, and packet counts.
Shows TCP offload state. Useful when troubleshooting NIC offload/acceleration issues.
Displays all connections, listening ports, and bound non-listening TCP ports. Helps spot sockets in a bound state without a listener.

common_errors.description: Occurs when using options like -b (show executable) without an elevated Command Prompt. Run as Administrator.
Seen with netstat -b when the tool cannot map a socket to an executable (insufficient rights or the process exited). Try elevation and rerun promptly.
Name resolution delays when not using -n or when using -f to resolve FQDNs. Use -n to disable lookups or ensure DNS is responsive.
Using an unsupported protocol token (e.g., netstat -p foo). Use one of: TCP, UDP, TCPv6, UDPv6, IP, IPv6, ICMP, ICMPv6.
Normal condition when there are no current TCP sessions. Verify service is listening (-a) or traffic is present.

common_errors.error: 'netstat' is not recognized as an internal or external command...
common_errors.description: PATH/environment issue or severely minimal Windows environment. Ensure %SystemRoot%\System32 is in PATH and the binary exists.

explanation.title: Understanding the command
explanation.purpose: netstat surfaces real-time socket, listener, and routing information, letting technicians verify whether services are listening, identify which processes own ports, and assess TCP/UDP activity and protocol health.
explanation.when_to_use: Use when diagnosing port-in-use errors, confirming if a service is listening, mapping connections to processes, investigating unexpected remote connections, inspecting TCP state anomalies (e.g., CLOSE_WAIT spikes), checking routing tables, or reviewing protocol statistics.

what_to_check.name: Listeners on expected ports
what_to_check.description: Verify that required services show LISTENING on the correct Local Address and port (e.g., 0.0.0.0:443 or 127.0.0.1:5432).

what_to_check.name: Owning PID (-o) and executable (-b)
what_to_check.description: Confirms which process/binary holds a port so you can correlate with service configurations or terminate the right process.

what_to_check.name: TCP states
what_to_check.description: Look for excessive CLOSE_WAIT, TIME_WAIT, or SYN_SENT which can indicate application issues, high churn, or reachability problems.

what_to_check.name: Foreign endpoints
what_to_check.description: Identify unexpected remote IPs or an unusual volume of ESTABLISHED sessions to potential suspicious destinations.

what_to_check.name: Routing table (-r)
what_to_check.description: Confirm correct default gateway and route metrics if connectivity works to some networks but not others.

what_to_check.name: Protocol statistics (-s)
what_to_check.description: High retransmits, resets, or errors in TCP/UDP can indicate congestion, packet loss, or misconfiguration.

what_to_check.name: Offload state (-t)
what_to_check.description: Determine whether NIC offload features are active for connections when investigating performance anomalies.

interpretation.title: Many sockets in CLOSE_WAIT
interpretation.message: Remote peers closed, but the local app did not close its side. Investigate the application holding sockets open; consider restarts or patches.

interpretation.title: High TIME_WAIT counts
interpretation.message: Normal after heavy outbound traffic, but persistent high counts can contribute to ephemeral port exhaustion. Review connection reuse and TIME_WAIT tuning.

interpretation.title: LISTENING on 0.0.0.0 or [::]
interpretation.message: Service is exposed on all interfaces. Validate firewall rules and intended exposure scope.

interpretation.title: SYN_SENT without ESTABLISHED
interpretation.message: Outbound connection attempts are not completing. Check remote availability, firewall ACLs, routing, or packet loss.

interpretation.title: No listener on expected port
interpretation.message: Service likely not started, bound to localhost only, or port conflict exists. Verify service config and identify conflicting PID with -o.

explanation.common_mistake: Running netstat without -n during troubleshooting, leading to long delays from reverse DNS lookups and misinterpreting the pause as a network hang.
explanation.permissions_notes: Most netstat output is available to standard users. Options like -b (executable mapping) often require an elevated Command Prompt. Some entries may show 'Can not obtain ownership information' without admin rights or if the process exits quickly.
explanation.risk_warning: Read-only command; however, it may reveal sensitive process names, IPs, and ports in logs or screenshots. Use -n to avoid unnecessary DNS lookups on production systems.

next_steps.name: tasklist
next_steps.summary: Map PIDs from netstat -o to process names to identify the owning application.

next_steps.name: taskkill
next_steps.summary: Terminate a misbehaving process identified by netstat that is holding a required port.

next_steps.name: route
next_steps.summary: Inspect or adjust routes after reviewing netstat -r if traffic is taking an unexpected path.

next_steps.name: ping
next_steps.summary: Test basic reachability to a Foreign Address seen in netstat to confirm connectivity.

next_steps.name: tracert
next_steps.summary: Trace the network path to remote endpoints identified by netstat to locate routing or hop-by-hop issues.

next_steps.name: ipconfig
next_steps.summary: Verify local IP configuration (IP, DNS, gateway) if netstat shows unexpected bindings or routing issues.

explanation.narrative: Start with netstat -ano to list listeners and active connections with PIDs. If a required port is busy or missing, filter with findstr to confirm its state, then use -o to capture the PID and, if needed, -b (elevated) to see the executable. Check TCP states for symptoms like CLOSE_WAIT or SYN_SENT to guide whether the issue is application-side or network-side. Review netstat -r when pathing seems wrong. From there, correlate the PID with tasklist, adjust routes if necessary, or test the remote host with ping/tracert.
